claims.text: CoCrFeMnNi-based HEA multilayers can be used to isolate and observe a transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep.
The face-centered-cubic CoCrFeMnNi structure exhibits high-temperature stability.
Interactions between interfaces and the CoCrFeMnNi matrix influence creep mechanisms.
The proposed multilayers are fully dense and polycrystalline, with coherent and semicoherent interfaces and layer thicknesses from tens to hundreds of nanometers.
Adjusting the composition of adjoining CoCrFeMnNi-based layers varies their lattice mismatch.
Varying lattice mismatch alters interface coherency.
Thermomechanical testing at 600–900 °C can capture both diffusion-driven and dislocation-driven creep modes in these multilayers.
Interface coherency is governed by lattice misfit.
At higher temperatures and lower stresses, coherent interfaces hinder dislocation activity.
At higher temperatures and lower stresses, coherent interfaces favor interfacial diffusion and diffusion-dominated creep.
At lower temperatures and higher stresses, misfit dislocations form at semicoherent interfaces.
Misfit dislocations at semicoherent interfaces foster dislocation motion and cause dislocation-dominated creep.
Increasing stress produces a marked transition between creep regimes in CoCrFeMnNi.
The stress-induced transition is specifically from diffusion-controlled creep to dislocation-controlled creep.
Decreasing temperature produces a shift from diffusion-controlled to dislocation-controlled creep.
Interface coherency modulates the proposed creep-mechanism transition.
Monolithic CoCrFeMnNi exhibits dislocation-based creep across the proposed temperature range.
Interfacial chemistry and grain-size effects can obscure the influence of interface coherency on creep.
